title: From the Diary of Anne Frank (poem: Amanda!)

learn.hook: A diary is the one friend who listens to everything and never interrupts.
points: 'From the Diary of Anne Frank' comes from the diary of a Jewish girl who got it on her 13th birthday in 1942 and named it Kitty.
She felt she had no true friend to confide in, so the diary became that friend. In school her teacher Mr Keesing gave her extra essays for talking too much in class.
Diary format: date, day and time at the top; 'Dear Diary' (optional); body; your name at the end.
A diary is personal and informal, written in the first person (I, me, my).
Write what happened (mostly past tense) AND how you felt about it.

example.q: Diary: Monday, 3 March, 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today Miss Iyer made me read my poem aloud. My voice shook at first, but the whole class clapped! I might write another one tonight. — Pihu What two things does a good diary entry like this contain?
steps: Events: Pihu read her poem aloud and the class clapped.
Feelings: her voice shook (nervous), then 'clapped!' shows joy.
Format: date, day, time, 'Dear Diary', name at the end.
example.answer: What happened (events) and how the writer felt (feelings), in the proper diary format.

learn.reallife: Many people keep a journal or gratitude diary; even a scientist's lab notebook and a ship captain's logbook are kinds of diaries.

games.title: Diary facts
items: A diary entry is written in the first person.
It uses I, me and my.
A diary entry must have a formal subject line like a letter.
Subject lines belong to formal letters, not diaries.
Anne Frank named her diary Kitty.
Anne got her diary on her 13th birthday.
It was a birthday gift in June 1942.
A diary records only events, never feelings.
Feelings are at the heart of a diary.
Mr Keesing gave Anne extra essays because she talked too much in class.
He wanted to punish her chattering, but she wrote cleverly.

quiz.q: What name did Anne Frank give her diary?
quiz.explain: Anne addressed her diary as 'Kitty', like a friend.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the diary's name with a family member's name

quiz.q: Why did Anne decide to keep a diary?
options: She felt she had no true friend to confide in
She wanted to become a journalist
She had nothing to do at school
quiz.explain: She had many acquaintances but no real friend to share her thoughts with.
quiz.mistake: Gives a common reason that is not in the lesson

quiz.q: Why did Mr Keesing give Anne extra essays to write?
options: She talked too much in class
quiz.explain: He kept punishing her chattering with extra essays.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a reason linked to studies

quiz.q: What goes at the very top of a diary entry?
quiz.explain: A diary begins with the date, day and time.
quiz.mistake: Mixes diary format with formal-letter format

quiz.q: A diary entry is usually written in which person?
quiz.explain: The writer speaks about herself or himself: I, me, my.
quiz.mistake: Thinks diaries are written like stories about others

quiz.q: What is the tone of a diary entry?
quiz.explain: A diary is a private conversation with oneself.
quiz.mistake: Applies letter-writing rules to diaries

quiz.q: Diary: Monday, 3 March, 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today Miss Iyer made me read my poem aloud. My voice shook at first, but the whole class clapped! I might write another one tonight. — Pihu What made Pihu happy?
options: Miss Iyer gave her a prize
The whole class clapped for her poem
She did not have to read
quiz.explain: She writes that the whole class clapped, followed by an exclamation mark.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the word 'but', which shows the change from nervous to happy

quiz.q: Diary: Monday, 3 March, 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today Miss Iyer made me read my poem aloud. My voice shook at first, but the whole class clapped! I might write another one tonight. — Pihu Which detail of diary format is missing in Pihu's entry?
quiz.explain: The entry has the day, date, time, 'Dear Diary', the body and her name.
quiz.mistake: Does not check the top and bottom of the entry

teach.ask: Gappu: I want to start a diary! What do I write at the top, and what should go inside?
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Date on top, and my events AND feelings inside, all in 'I'. Dear Diary, here I come!
teach.nudge: What goes at the top of an entry, and besides events, what else should you write about?

learn.hook: A small notebook hidden in an attic became one of the most-read books in the world.
points: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945.
During the war, Jews were persecuted by the Nazis. Anne's family, who lived in Amsterdam, went into hiding in a secret part of a building from 1942 to 1944.
Anne did not survive the war. Her father, Otto Frank, published her diary, which has been translated into many languages.
Reporting yes/no questions: use 'asked + if/whether' and change to statement order: He asked, 'Are you ready?' → He asked if I was ready.
Reporting wh-questions: keep the wh-word and use statement order, no question mark: She asked, 'Where do you live?' → She asked me where I lived.

example.q: Report this: Mr Keesing asked Anne, 'Why are you talking again?'
steps: It is a wh-question, so keep 'why'.
Use statement order: subject before verb ('she was talking').
Shift the tense back: are → was; 'you' becomes 'she'; drop the question mark.
example.answer: Mr Keesing asked Anne why she was talking again.

learn.reallife: Interviewers and reporters often write questions this way: 'The reporter asked the minister when the bridge would open.'

items.text: She asked me ___ I had eaten lunch.
He asked me where the station ___.
Dad asked us when we ___ come home.
The teacher asked Anne why she ___ talking.
Riya asked her friend ___ she liked the book.

quiz.q: In which years was the Second World War fought?
quiz.explain: WWII began in 1939 and ended in 1945; 1914-1918 was the First World War.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the two world wars or the hiding period with the war

quiz.q: In which city did Anne Frank's family go into hiding?
quiz.explain: The family lived and hid in Amsterdam in the Netherlands.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they hid in Germany because Anne was born there

quiz.q: Who published Anne Frank's diary after the war?
quiz.explain: Her father survived and published her diary.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that Anne did not survive the war

quiz.q: Report: Mr Keesing asked Anne, 'Are you talking again?'
options: Mr Keesing asked Anne that she was talking again.
Mr Keesing asked Anne whether was she talking again?
Mr Keesing asked Anne are you talking again.
Mr Keesing asked Anne whether she was talking again.
quiz.explain: A yes/no question is reported with 'whether', statement order and no question mark.
quiz.mistake: Keeps question order or uses 'that' for a question

quiz.q: Report: She asked me, 'Where do you live?'
options: She asked me where I lived.
She asked me where do I live.
She asked me where did I live?
She asked me that where I live.
quiz.explain: Keep 'where', put subject before verb, and shift live → lived.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the question form 'do I live'

quiz.q: Which word introduces a reported yes/no question?
quiz.explain: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' or 'whether'.
quiz.mistake: Uses 'that', which is for reported statements

quiz.q: Report: The principal said to Rohan, 'Why are you late?'
options: The principal said Rohan why are you late.
The principal asked Rohan why was he late.
The principal asked Rohan why he was late.
The principal told Rohan that why he is late.
quiz.explain: 'Said to' becomes 'asked' for a question; then wh-word + statement order.
quiz.mistake: Keeps 'said' and the question word order

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: He asked me where was the station.
He asked me where is the station?
He asked me that where the station was.
He asked me where the station was.
quiz.explain: In reported questions the subject comes before the verb: 'the station was'.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the inverted question order

teach.ask: Gappu: Mummy asked me, 'Have you eaten?' How do I tell Papa what she asked?
teach.praise: Tweet! 'Mummy asked if I had eaten.' Use 'if', no question mark. I'm a reporting expert!
teach.nudge: Which word do you use for a yes/no question, and what happens to the question mark?

learn.hook: 'Do this! Don't do that!' Ever wished you could fly away from all the instructions?
points: 'Amanda!' by Robin Klein shows a girl who is given non-stop instructions; she escapes in her imagination into daydreams of freedom, such as being a mermaid or Rapunzel.
The poem's message: children need some freedom and space, not constant nagging.
Sentence types: declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request), exclamatory (strong feeling).
Imperative sentences usually begin with a verb and have an understood 'you': 'Sit straight!', 'Don't shout.'
In poems like this, lines in brackets can show a child's inner thoughts.

example.q: Poem: Sit straight, Ishaan! Don't swing your feet! / (I'm a falcon over Ladakh's peaks.) / Finish your milk and comb your hair! / (Up here there's only sky and air.) What do the lines in brackets show?
steps: The other lines are commands: Sit straight! Finish your milk!
The bracketed lines describe flying over Ladakh, which Ishaan is not really doing.
So they are his daydreams, his escape from the instructions.
example.answer: They show Ishaan's imagination: he daydreams of being free while being given orders.

learn.reallife: Hobbies, outdoor play and free time help children relax and think creatively.

quiz.q: Who wrote the poem 'Amanda!'?
quiz.explain: 'Amanda!' is by Robin Klein.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up poets of First Flight

quiz.q: Why does Amanda daydream of being a mermaid or Rapunzel?
options: Because she wants to swim in a competition
To escape the constant instructions and feel free
quiz.explain: Her daydreams are an escape from nagging into a world of freedom.
quiz.mistake: Reads the daydreams literally as wishes for a hobby

quiz.q: In 'Amanda!', who is most likely giving Amanda all the instructions?
quiz.explain: The commands about manners and chores come from an adult at home, usually taken to be her mother.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the speaker with the characters in Amanda's daydreams

quiz.q: Poem: Sit straight, Ishaan! Don't swing your feet! / (I'm a falcon over Ladakh's peaks.) / Finish your milk and comb your hair! / (Up here there's only sky and air.) What do the lines in brackets show?
quiz.explain: They describe flying over Ladakh, which happens only in his imagination.
quiz.mistake: Takes the imagined flight as real

quiz.q: What type of sentence is 'Don't swing your feet!'?
quiz.explain: It gives a command; the exclamation mark adds force but it is still an imperative.
quiz.mistake: Judges the type only by the exclamation mark

quiz.q: Which is an exclamatory sentence?
quiz.explain: It expresses a strong feeling and begins with 'What a ...'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with an order is exclamatory

quiz.q: What does 'nag' mean?
quiz.explain: To nag is to keep finding fault or telling someone what to do.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with an unrelated word

quiz.q: Poem: Sit straight, Ishaan! Don't swing your feet! / (I'm a falcon over Ladakh's peaks.) / Finish your milk and comb your hair! / (Up here there's only sky and air.) What is the tone of the lines that are not in brackets?
quiz.explain: They are a stream of commands, which sounds bossy.
quiz.mistake: Mixes the tone of the commands with the tone of the daydreams

teach.ask: Gappu: Mama Bird keeps saying 'Sit straight! Eat your worm!' What kind of sentences are those, and why do I daydream?
teach.praise: Chirp! Those are imperative sentences, and daydreams are my escape to freedom. Just like Amanda!
teach.nudge: What do we call a sentence that gives an order? And why does the child daydream?
